sermon:
## Everything You Need, and the Word You Can Trust
*What God has already given, and why you can stake your life on the page that says so*

**Text:** 2 Peter 1:1-21 · **Supporting:** Acts 1:8 · Romans 5:3-5 · 1 Peter 1:10-12 · Mark 9:2-8

Peter is an old man writing his last letter, and he knows it. He says so a few lines in, "I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me" (2 Peter 1:14). A man who knows he is dying does not waste words on the inessential. So watch what he reaches for at the end. Not a final strategy. Not a clever defense. He reaches for what God has already done, and for the word he is leaving behind.

**He has already given you everything. You are not waiting on God.**
Read the opening claim slowly, because everything else in the letter stands on it. "His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence" (2 Peter 1:3). Not some things. All things. Not will grant, has granted. The verb is past tense and it is finished. The Christian does not stand at the bottom of a ladder of requirements, hoping to accumulate enough of God's favor to be admitted. The Christian stands inside a gift already given, holding what he has not yet learned to use.

We do not believe this. We say we do, and then we live like spiritual beggars, scanning the horizon for some new experience, some conference, some technique that will finally produce the godliness we assume is being withheld. Peter calls that exactly backward. The power is already in the house. He goes further, "he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4). The God who made you is not rationing himself. The lack you feel is not a lack in his supply.

**Now add yourself to what he gave. Confirm it. Make it sure.**
Here is where the comfortable reading breaks. Because if everything is given, the lazy mind concludes there is nothing to do. Peter will not let that stand. "For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness, and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love" (2 Peter 1:5-7). The gift does not cancel the effort. The gift is the reason for the effort. You build on what you cannot manufacture.

The chain is not random. It climbs. Faith without virtue is only assent. Virtue without knowledge is blind sincerity. Knowledge without self-control is a man who knows the truth and cannot keep his appetites from contradicting it. The word under steadfastness is *hupomonē*, endurance under weight, the staying-power of a man who does not put the load down when it gets heavy. Paul knew the same chain runs the same direction: "suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope" (Romans 5:3-4). And Peter's warning is plain about the alternative. "Whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins" (2 Peter 1:9). The man who stops adding does not merely stall. He forgets the cross that cleansed him. So the great command lands: "be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall" (2 Peter 1:10). Confirm it. Not earn it, confirm it. Make sure to yourself the thing God has already made sure to himself.

I have stood in a pulpit and preached a gift that costs nothing and asks nothing, because it is easier to comfort a room than to summon one. I have let people believe that because grace is free, growth is optional. Peter is rebuking the man who taught it. The believer is to add himself, his discipline, his endurance, his slow accumulation of character, to the salvation he could never buy. Both are true at once. He gave it all. And you are still on the hook to grow.

**Why you can stake your life on the page that tells you so.**
Strip the foundation out and the whole thing collapses. So Peter ends by telling you why the word you are reading can be trusted with your soul. He was there. "We did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty" (2 Peter 1:16). He saw the Transfiguration with his own eyes, the face changed, the garments white, the voice from the cloud: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (2 Peter 1:17; Mark 9:7). An old man on the edge of death is staking his last words on a thing he watched happen on a mountain.

But he does not stop at his own eyes. He points to something more durable than memory. "We have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place" (2 Peter 1:19). And then the line the whole church has built its confidence on: "no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation. For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit" (2 Peter 1:20-21). *Carried along.* The same word a ship's sail knows when the wind takes it. The prophets did not invent. They were borne. Peter the eyewitness tells you that the page in your hand outranks even what he saw, because the Spirit who carried Moses and Isaiah is the same Spirit who guarantees the gift.

This is where the patient certainty of the whole letter is quietly planted. The Christ who was glorified on the mountain is the Christ who is coming, Peter calls it "the power and coming of our Lord" in the same breath. And the lamp shines in a dark place "until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts" (2 Peter 1:19). The day has not dawned. We are still in the dark place, still holding the lamp, still adding to our faith while the light delays. The waiting is not abandonment. The lamp was given for the dark. The morning star has not yet risen, and the man who knows that does not stop building, he builds harder, because the One who promised is the One who already gave everything and will not be slow to finish it.

He gave it all. Add yourself.

## False Teachers and the Judgment That Waits
*Why the most dangerous threat to the church has always come from inside it, and why its sentence is not asleep*

**Text:** 2 Peter 2:1-22 · **Supporting:** Jude 1:4 · Genesis 19:24-25 · Matthew 7:15 · 2 Timothy 4:3

Peter has just told you the prophetic word is sure. Now he tells you what will be done to it. The same sentence holds both halves: "But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you" (2 Peter 2:1). Among the people, and among you. The lie does not break in through the windows. It is ordained a deacon. It is given a microphone. It sits in the second pew and teaches the class. Peter's warning is not about the world outside the walls. It is about the man who shares your communion.

**They come in quietly, and they come in for money.**
Notice how Peter says they arrive. "Who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction" (2 Peter 2:1). Secretly. Not with a banner that reads heresy. No one announces that he has come to dismantle the church. He comes in beside you, agreeing with most of it, smiling, useful, and then, slowly, "denying the Master who bought them." The denial is rarely a frontal assault on the creed. It is a quiet relocation of the center, away from the Master and toward the self.

And Peter names the engine. "And in their greed they will exploit you with false words" (2 Peter 2:3). Greed and sensuality, again and again, "many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed" (2 Peter 2:2). The false teacher is not primarily a man with bad theology. He is a man with an appetite, who has discovered that the church will feed it. Jude, writing almost the same warning, names the same men, "ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ" (Jude 4). Paul saw it coming at the church and at himself: "the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions" (2 Timothy 4:3). The frightening part of that verse is who does the accumulating. Not the teachers. The people. We hire the men who tell us what our appetites already decided.

I have watched a congregation choose the comfortable man over the true one, and I have wanted to be the comfortable man, because the comfortable man is loved and paid and invited back. Peter is not describing a stranger. He is describing a pull I feel in my own chest every time I prepare to say a hard thing to people I need to keep liking me. The way of truth gets blasphemed not only by the wolf. It gets blasphemed by the shepherd who decided to keep the peace.

**God has a record, and the record is not sentimental.**
Then Peter does the thing the false teacher never expects. He opens the ledger of history. "For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment; if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah... when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly; if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly" (2 Peter 2:4-6). Three cases. The angels who outranked us. The whole ancient world. The cities so confident in their corruption they could not imagine an accounting. Genesis records what their confidence bought them, "the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire... and he overthrew those cities" (Genesis 19:24-25).

The argument is a single hammer-blow: if God did not spare the angels, the world, or the cities, what makes the false teacher think he is the exception? Judgment is not a threat Peter invented to frighten the timid. It is a documented pattern. The God of the page Peter just defended is the God who has acted, who has a court, who keeps records that do not get lost.

But the same ledger holds the other column, and you must not miss it. The God who did not spare also *did* spare. "Then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment" (2 Peter 2:9). Noah was preserved. Lot was pulled out, "righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked" (2 Peter 2:7). The same competence that condemns the wolf rescues the sheep. God knows how to do both, and he does both, and he has never once gotten the two confused.

**The judgment waits, and the waiting is not weakness.**
Here is the line that holds your whole faith together. The unrighteous are kept "under punishment until the day of judgment." Until. The sentence has been passed. The execution is delayed. And that delay is precisely what the false teacher counts on. He looks around, sees the floor not opening beneath him, the money still coming in, the congregation still applauding, and he concludes there is no judge. He reads the patience of God as the absence of God.

He is reading it exactly wrong. Peter's most haunting image is what these men actually are: "waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved" (2 Peter 2:17). A spring with no water. A man who promises living water and leaves the thirsty thirsty. And the most sobering verdict in the chapter, "it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back" (2 Peter 2:21). These are not pagans who never heard. These are insiders who tasted and turned.

The certain return of the Master who bought them is the whole hinge. The judgment is not asleep, it is reserved, held, scheduled. The cross of the Master they deny is the very thing they trample, and the day is coming when the patience that delayed the sentence runs out. This is the costly comfort for the faithful and the terror for the wolf: the same delay that lets the false teacher keep preaching is the mercy of a God who is not slow, only patient, and patience is not the same thing as forgetting. Christ delays. Christ does not fail to come.

Their judgment is not asleep.

## The Day Will Come, So Grow
*Why the silence of heaven is not the absence of God, and what to do while you wait*

**Text:** 2 Peter 3:1-18 · **Supporting:** Psalm 90:4 · 1 Thessalonians 5:2 · Romans 2:4 · Habakkuk 2:3

This is the last thing Peter says before he dies, and he says it to people who are starting to wonder if they were fooled. The promise was that Christ would come. The years have passed. The fathers who first believed it are in their graves now, and the world looks exactly as it always did. Into that quiet doubt Peter writes, not to scold the doubt, but to answer it.

**The scoffer's question is older than you think, and it has an answer.**
Peter names the mockery in the mocker's own voice, because he is not afraid of it. "Scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, 'Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation'" (2 Peter 3:3-4). It is a serious question and it deserves a serious answer. Nothing has changed. The kettle still boils, the sun still rises, the funeral processions still pass. Where is the promised end of all this?

But notice what Peter says drives the question, "following their own sinful desires." The scoffer is not a neutral philosopher who weighed the evidence and found it wanting. He is a man who wants the Judge not to come, and has talked himself into the comfort of his preference. There is a kernel of truth in his observation, the world does look continuous, the delay is real. But the conclusion is motivated, not measured. He prefers an absent God because a present one has a claim on his desires. And his memory is conveniently short. "They deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God, and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished" (2 Peter 3:5-6). The man who says God has never intervened has forgotten the flood. The continuity he is counting on was already broken once.

**God does not keep your clock. He keeps his promise.**
Then Peter answers the delay with the only thing that actually answers it. "But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day" (2 Peter 3:8). He is quoting the prayer of Moses, "a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past" (Psalm 90:4). We are measuring God's faithfulness with a wristwatch. We feel the years drag and conclude the promise has failed, when the truth is that the One who made time is not standing inside it tapping his foot the way we are.

And then the verse that turns the whole thing on its head. "The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance" (2 Peter 3:9). The delay you have been reading as failure is mercy. Every year the Judge does not come is a year the door stays open. Paul asked the question that exposes the heart: "do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?" (Romans 2:4). The patience you complain about is the only reason you are still inside the offer. Habakkuk waited too, and was told the same thing, "if it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come, it will not delay" (Habakkuk 2:3).

I have prayed for God to act and resented the silence, calling his patience neglect. I have wanted the Judge to come down hard on the people I had already condemned, and never once stopped to think that I was on the wrong side of that delay, that the mercy keeping them out of judgment was the same mercy that once waited for me. The scoffer and the impatient believer make the same mistake from opposite ends. Both read the waiting as God's weakness. It is God's restraint, aimed at someone's salvation, and it may be aimed at someone you love.

**The day will come, so build like a man who believes it.**
But mercy delays the day. It does not cancel it. Peter is brutally clear. "But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed" (2 Peter 3:10). Paul said the same of the timing, "the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2). It will come unannounced and it will come completely. The continuity the scoffer trusts will end in a single hour.

And here is the turn the whole letter has been building toward, not panic, not chart-making, not a survivalist's bunker. "Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God?" (2 Peter 3:11-12). The certainty that it all burns is not an excuse to disengage. It is the reason to be holy. We are "waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells" (2 Peter 3:13), and the man who truly waits for that does not kill time. He grows. Peter's final command is the same one he opened with, now under the weight of the coming fire: "grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ" (2 Peter 3:18).

This is the whole tension of the Christian life held in one chapter. The day is certain, the Christ who was glorified on the mountain is coming to judge and to remake. The day is delayed, and the delay is mercy, the patience of a God who is not willing that any should perish. So the faithful do not stand at the window waiting for the sky to crack. They grow. They add to their faith. They confirm their calling. They live holy lives in a world that is going to burn, because they believe the One who promised to come is the same One who already gave them everything they needed to be ready. The silence of heaven is not the absence of God. It is the open door, and it will not stay open forever.

Mercy delays it. Grow meanwhile.
